#6256. Why New Runways Do Not Always Increase An Airport's Flight Capacity

Airport infrastructure projects have been a hot topic this year. From Australia to Asia to the Middle East to the United States, new airport openings and expansions are in progress across the world. In any case, building or even adding to each airport will have been a far more complicated process than it may have appeared on the surface.

In particular, planners have to carefully consider an eye-watering number of factors when building a runway alone. Where there is another runway in operation close by, the task becomes even more difficult. Simply put, it is by no means a matter of laying the groundwork and letting the aircraft move in.

The harsh truth for airport operators has previously been summed up by global trade association Airports Council International (ACI). “The capacity provided by the airport system is determined by multiple factors, many of which are not directly within an airport operator’s control,” it wrote in a 2019 research paper relating to air operations in Europe. These factors primarily include an airport’s runway or runways, its apron, terminal infrastructure, and the surrounding airspace.

While planners may have full autonomy over where runways are positioned and how many there are, a lack of apron space for aircraft to move about or park on the ground could prevent the landing strips from operating at full capacity, for instance. Similarly, terminal space may be plentiful, but busy local airspace may mean air movements are capped, so the number of passengers that could in theory be processed by an airport will never be met.

All of that goes to say that each factor matters for lifting capacity, but it can only do so in practice if the other considerations are addressed. Local airspace restrictions are arguably the trickiest for airports to navigate. Authorities can plan and lay out infrastructure on the ground as well as possible, but the traffic that can actually use it will be dependent on what is nearby. Its own designated controlled airspace — or Terminal Maneuvering Area — might overlap another airport’s, say, or something as simple as noise restrictions could be in place and so limit operations at certain times. When adding runways, planners must consider these factors before breaking ground.

Among the most obvious constraints to growing capacity by opening a new runway is the airport itself. That stretches beyond just aprons and terminals. Whether it be public transport, roads, or car parking spaces, getting passengers on and off site is one issue. Add in the need for additional check-in counters, security checkpoints, passenger waiting areas, and aircraft docking gates, and more flights will mean more stress on every part of an airport.

There is no solid guarantee that building all of that will drastically improve capacity, too. According to a 1982 Congressional study, efforts undertaken in response to growing demand for flights tended to have the largest impact on reducing delays. Of course, where new long runways are built and properly equipped for independent flight rules (IFR) operations, capacity could increase. That said, factors such as the original runway configuration meant that the jump could be anywhere in the region of 20% to 50%.

While potentially significant, the cost and effort behind building an extra runway could deem the entire project unviable. An 11,000-foot (3,353-meter) runway with its basic safety area covered 130 acres (52.6 hectares), the study noted. Combined with other necessary clear zones, the area directly affected stretched to three or four times that. To put that space to work, the airport had to bring the rest of its infrastructure up to scratch. All of that effort risked going to waste when the other existing landing strip or strips were taken into consideration as well.

Runways impact an aircraft performance when looking to take off and land.

Outside upgrading airport infrastructure and building a new runway, its location relative to existing operational strips is key. Where two or more runways run parallel, spacing between aircraft making approaches in the same direction at the same time must be ensured. Such simultaneous same-direction operations, as the United States’ Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) dubs them, require visual flight rules (VFR) conditions, maintained two‐way radio communication with each aircraft involved, and a minimum distance between the centerlines of each runway.

Where heavy aircraft — so widebodies like the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 — were involved, that minimum distance was historically 700 feet (213 meters). Changes brought in earlier this year have since required such close approaches to be staggered. Either way, using runways in close proximity simultaneously relies on good weather. Poor conditions can require much greater distances between adjacent aircraft. At airports with precision runway monitor (PRM) systems that allow simultaneous instrument approaches, a distance of 2,500 feet (762 meters) is needed between landing strips. If not available, that figure can stretch to 4,300 feet (1,311 meters).

Naturally, these rules reduce the risk of aircraft straying into each other’s paths, including in instances of go-arounds. They also ensure air disturbed by one, known as wake turbulence, does not destabilize another. Wake turbulence can be powerful enough to flip a pursuing or nearby aircraft in extreme cases. Sometimes, however, the vicinity of one runway to another is just too close, and extra runways do not always equate to additional capacity.

According to the FAA, just four airports globally conduct PRM approaches as it stands: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), and Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD). Elsewhere, when parallel runways are too close, air traffic controllers can be limited in how they handle arrivals and departures, especially in the event of bad weather.

San Francisco International Airport (SFO) offers a prime example. Though it has two sets of parallel runways, they sit just 750 feet (229 meters) apart from each other in each direction. The airport had been allowed to use each adjacent set simultaneously until recently, before the FAA effectively banned the practice in response to a fatal crash in Washington, DC, last year.

This allowed a maximum arrival rate of around 54 aircraft per hour. Now, though, all aircraft flying into the airport must follow a staggered, diagonal sequence along the final approach path. That, in turn, has reduced the arrival rate to about 45 per hour currently, even in fair conditions. During periods of poor visibility, that drops further to 36 landings an hour as arriving aircraft are placed in a single-file pattern. Needless to say, the vicinity of the two sets of parallel runways at SFO has done little to aid capacity of late. Even without bad weather, other issues can severely constrain operations around airports, regardless of the number of runways available.

How Gatwick handles over 43 million passengers annually with one runway through world-class scheduling, rapid turnarounds, and operational efficiency.

Behind all the physical infrastructure needed for an airport to grow capacity are the humans to run it. Responsibility for how runway systems are managed ultimately falls to air traffic controllers. That is, selecting an appropriate configuration and sequencing flights to use falls to those in the control towers.

When multiple landing strips are in play, that all becomes more complex and may even require additional monitoring positions. Any shortage of air traffic control personnel can limit the feasible set of configurations available at an airport as a result, as concluded in a 2026 review of runway systems published in MDPI.

Unfortunately, such shortages are a global issue today. An aging workforce and high training requirements are said to have driven a trend of cross-border recruitment across the industry, per Reuters. Staff shortages have already contributed to flight disruptions in major markets like Australia, the US, and Canada; meanwhile, estimates call for 71,000 new air traffic controllers across the world by 2034 in order to meet demand. Without them, airports' efforts to increase capacity risk becoming obsolete.

So, simply building a new runway is by no means the only thing airport officials have to consider when looking to increase the number of flights they can process. London Heathrow Airport (LHR) is one site where the debate around adding a strip has been long-running. Considered to be among the most slot-constrained airports in the world, Heathrow is in the process of seeking planning permission for its expansion.

In its case, the UK government has laid out key tests that any solid plan will be assessed against. That includes the expansion's economic impact, environmental cost, and compliance with air quality and noise regulations. Again, that means further considerations outside of actually building the runway, synchronizing operations, upgrading infrastructure at the site, and whether there will be enough air traffic controllers when the time comes — which really affects capacity.

#6255. The 6 Best Airplane Bathrooms On Any Airline: The A380 Reigns Supreme

When most people think of airplane bathrooms, it’s probably not a nice image that comes to mind. Airlines have largely shrunk bathrooms on newer aircraft significantly, and at times they’re also not very well maintained.

That’s not true across the board, though. In premium cabins, we’ve seen airlines introduce some pretty amazing amenities in recent years, and that even includes awesome bathrooms.

In this post, I’d like to share what I consider to be the airlines with the best first class bathrooms (somewhat overlapping with my list of the world’s best first class airlines).

Unsurprisingly, the Airbus A380 takes center stage on this flight, as it’s an aircraft that has ushered in the most bathroom innovation. That’s because the front of the upper deck has a bit of extra space that can’t be utilized for seats, making room for some cool amenities.

With that in mind, below are my six favorite airplane bathrooms, roughly ranked…

Emirates A380 first class is one of my all-around favorite first class products, and a large part of that is the amazing A380 first class shower suites.

Emirates’ A380s have two first class shower suites at the front of the upper deck, equipped with heated floors, enough amenities to start a toiletry resale business, and most importantly, a shower.

As a first class passenger, you can schedule a shower at the beginning of your flight, and while there’s no time limit to how long you can use the shower spa, you’re limited to five minutes of water. Fortunately you can turn the water on and off without the clock “running,” so that’s more than enough water for a nice shower.

Of all the excitement I’ve experienced in the air, I don’t think anything compares to the first time I took a shower on Emirates. The airline even has shower spa attendants, who make sure the shower spas are well maintained throughout the flight.

Etihad A380 first class consists of nine “First Class Apartments,” and these passengers have access to the shower suite at the front of the cabin. Much like on Emirates, each passenger gets five minutes of water, and the shower suite is refreshed between each use.

While this is a great and refreshing feature, the shower suite definitely isn’t as spacious as on Emirates. So if you’re used to showering on Emirates, you might find that it’s a bit tight, but otherwise you’ll no doubt be delighted. Also keep in mind that there’s still The Residence on Etihad, which is a three room suite that can be reserved as an upgrade over the standard first class. This comes with a private bathroom, including shower.

Singapore Airlines A380 Suites is an incredible first class product, with only six seats in the cabin. While you won’t find a shower on Singapore Airlines’ A380s, you will find some of the most spacious bathrooms in the sky. One of the lavatories has a huge vanity, and is probably the size of 10 typical Boeing 737 MAX bathrooms. Airplane bathrooms don’t get much more luxurious than this!

Qatar Airways A380 first class has two very nice lavatories at the front of the upper deck. While there aren’t any special amenities, you’ll find that they’re incredibly spacious, and nicely decorated.

Lufthansa A380 first class features two huge lavatories at the front of the upper deck, each equipped with a bench, and most excitingly, a urinal! Lufthansa is the only airline to offer urinals on planes, so that’s pretty special… or something.

While we’re speaking of Lufthansa, I have a soft spot for Lufthansa 747-8 first class, probably at least partly because the Boeing 747-8 is my favorite plane as an avgeek. While not quite as over the top as some of the other options, Lufthansa’s 747-8 lavatories are spacious, have a bench you can extend out over the toilet, and most importantly, have a window. It’s so nice to be able to look out the window while in the lavatory.

Lastly on the topic of Lufthansa and lavatories, I do have to bring up how cool the economy lavatories on the carrier’s A340-600s were (these planes were just recently retired). They were located on the “lower deck” (in a cargo compartment), so they were probably the most unusual lavatories you could’ve recently found in commercial service. By comparison, the Lufthansa A340 first class lavatories weren’t much to get excited about at all.

All Nippon Airways A380 first class has two large, identical lavatories at the front of the upper deck. They’re huge, but there are also a couple of thoughtful design touches that I appreciate about them.

For one, ANA has a bidet function for its toilets, which is always a nice feature to have. I also appreciate how there’s a “plank” of sorts that you can extend on the ground, for situations where you want to change into pajamas without touching the regular floor of the bathroom.

On top of that, ANA does an amazing job with keeping its lavatories clean between each use, down to folding the toilet paper into perfect triangles.

Now, in fairness, there are a decent number of products with a bidet function in service, from Japan Airlines A350 first class, to Gulf Air 787 business class, to Oman Air 787 business class.

There are some pretty incredible airplane bathrooms out there. While nothing can compete with Emirates’ amazing shower suites, there are plenty of other impressive airplane bathrooms out there as well, with everything from vanities, to bidets, to urinals. As A380s increasingly get retired, unfortunately going to the bathroom on a plane is getting less pleasant!

What’s your favorite bathroom on a commercial aircraft?

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

They say the best deals never last forever, and in the world of points and miles, that's unquestionably true.

And after a pretty great run, one of the best deals in travel is about to get much harder to earn.

Thanks to major changes coming to Southwest Rapid Rewards in 2027, the days of using big credit card welcome bonuses to quickly earn a Southwest Companion Pass are almost over.

That's a big deal because the Companion Pass lets you bring a designated companion along on Southwest flights for just the cost of taxes and fees, starting at $5.60 each way. And you can use it again and again and again while your pass is valid.

But there's some good news if you've been hoping to earn one the quick and easy way.

You still have one last chance to use Southwest credit card welcome bonuses to help unlock a Companion Pass that's valid through the end of 2027. And the timing is especially good right now because Southwest just increased the welcome offers on its credit cards.

For example, the (see rates and fees) is currently offering 90,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

That's two-thirds of the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn a Companion Pass under the current rules, just from one welcome bonus.

There's just one catch: You need to apply and be approved for an eligible Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, to take advantage of this opportunity.

Here's how to make this strategy work one last time before the rules change.

Related: Southwest Rapid Rewards: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more

To earn a Southwest Companion Pass under the current rules, you need to earn 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year. Normally, all those points would need to post to your Southwest account by Dec. 31, but Southwest is making a special exception as it transitions to its new rules for 2027.

As long as you're approved for an eligible Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, its welcome-bonus points can still count toward qualification under the 2026 Companion Pass rules, even if they post in early 2027.

That means you have a little more time to meet the spending requirement and earn those bonus points. However, you still need to earn enough qualifying points from other eligible activities in 2026.

And importantly, if you aren't approved for a Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, the welcome bonus points won't count toward a Companion Pass under this special exception.

Here's an example of how this could work.

Let's say you've already earned 45,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in 2026 from flying Southwest or using eligible partners, such as hotels, rental cars and the Rapid Rewards shopping portal.

That leaves you needing another 90,000 qualifying points to unlock the pass — that's where the newly increased Southwest credit card offers come in.

If you apply for and are approved for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority Credit Card by Dec. 2, and then earn its 90,000-point welcome bonus after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months, you could have enough points to earn a Southwest Companion Pass valid through Dec. 31, 2027. The everyday spending you put on the card also earns points that can help you get closer to qualifying for the pass.

And once you earn the pass, you're able to bring your designated companion along on Southwest flights as often as you want in 2027, paying just the taxes and fees.

Of course, not everyone already has around 45,000 qualifying points earned in 2026. But there's potentially another way to earn enough points before this opportunity disappears.

The timing couldn't be much better if you're hoping to earn a Southwest Companion Pass before the rules change, as Southwest just increased the welcome offers on all five of its credit cards.

Here are the current offers to consider if you want to take advantage of this opportunity before the Dec. 2 deadline.

These are limited-time offers, and we don't yet know when they will end. And remember that you need to be approved by Dec. 2, 2026, to take advantage of the special rules allowing these welcome bonuses to count toward a Companion Pass under the current qualification requirements.

The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Let's say you aren't on track to earn enough points to qualify for a Southwest Companion Pass one last time with just the points from one Southwest credit card bonus.

A natural question from the creative set of points enthusiasts who want to go all-in on Southwest might be ... can you get two Southwest credit card bonuses to count in one year?

The short answer is yes — in one specific situation.

Under Chase's current application restrictions, you're generally ineligible for another Southwest personal card if you already hold one, and previous welcome bonuses can also affect your eligibility.

On top of that, you must have at least 24 months between Southwest personal card welcome bonuses. So if you got one in early 2026, you can't get another now in late 2026, even if you no longer have the first card.

However, having a Southwest personal card doesn't necessarily prevent you from qualifying for a Southwest business card, though Chase's 5/24 rule can still affect your eligibility.

The rules for Southwest business cards state that you cannot currently have that particular card and you cannot have received a welcome bonus on that particular card in the past 24 months.

So, depending on your eligibility, that means you could potentially combine the welcome bonuses from a Southwest personal card and a Southwest business card to earn enough points for a Companion Pass.

For example, the currently offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months, while the offers 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months.

That's a combined 140,000 bonus points, enough to reach the current 135,000-point Companion Pass threshold without even counting the points earned from meeting the spending requirements.

Southwest is in the process of dramatically reshaping its airline, its loyalty program and virtually everything in between. There will be lounges, a premium credit card and a more traditionally structured elite status program where the top tier comes with a Companion Pass.

And the credit cards will certainly play a large role in that reshaped airline well into the future.

But in the midst of all that change, we are looking down the barrel of a quickly approaching 'one last time' deadline if you want to get a Southwest credit card and have the welcome bonuses help you earn a Companion Pass.

Whether you're combining a bonus with points you've already earned or considering a personal and business card strategy, the key deadline is Dec. 2, 2026. You'll need to apply and be approved by then to take advantage of the special transition rules.

If you qualify, you could earn a Companion Pass valid through Dec. 31, 2027, allowing you to bring a designated companion on eligible Southwest flights for just the cost of taxes and fees.

#6252. Flagship Dining: American Expands A La Carte Lounge Dining To Business Class

Several weeks back, American announced plans to completely change the concept for its Flagship First Dining facilities, as the airline eliminates international first class. With this, we’re seeing Flagship First Dining simply rebranded as Flagship Dining, with business class passengers also getting access.

While these changes went “live” as of September 15, 2026, there’s now an additional update, as a third Flagship Dining facility has just opened, so you can now enjoy this experience in Dallas (DFW), Los Angeles (LAX), and Miami (MIA). Let’s cover all the details.

For years, American had Flagship First Dining, which are facilities inside select Flagship Lounges. The idea was that this offers an a la carte dining experience for those traveling in international or premium transcontinental first class.

American is currently in the process of eliminating “premium” first class — Boeing 777-300ERs are being reconfigured without first class, while Airbus A321XLRs (without first class) are replacing A321Ts. First class is no longer being sold on the wide bodies as of November 19, 2026, or on the narrow bodies as of March 28, 2027. So there has been a big question as to what American would do with these facilities in the future. Would they just close, or what? Well, it’s much better than that.

As of September 15, 2026, Flagship First Dining has simply become Flagship Dining, and the idea is that this is now open to all Flagship Business passengers traveling on qualifying long haul international, transcontinental, and Hawaii flights.

In other words, if you have access to a Flagship Lounge on account of your American business class ticket, you’re also eligible for Flagship Dining, on a space available basis. However, if you have Flagship Lounge access on account of elite status, or through traveling in a premium cabin on a partner airline, you wouldn’t have access to this facility.

American notes how guests interested in dining should check in with the host team inside the Flagship Lounge upon arrival. If a table is immediately available, guests will be seated at that time. If all tables are occupied, guests may be added to an electronic waitlist and will be notified when their table is ready. Tables will be offered on a first come, first served basis, and as I understand it, there’s no priority for first class passengers, Concierge Key members, etc.

I would expect that demand will greatly exceed supply, especially during peak hours. However, the same is true for the a la carte dining in United Polaris Lounges and (to a lesser extent) at some Delta One Lounges. This is really a great way for American to become more competitive with Delta and United. I’m really, really impressed, and this seems like a sincere effort to improve the premium experience.

Launching alongside the expanded dining facility access is an all-new four-course Flagship Dining menu. The airline promotes that “the seasonal offerings blend regional flavors, thoughtfully sourced ingredients and refined culinary techniques to create an elevated dining experience inspired by some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants.”

American is sharing some of the dishes that will be on offer, including a Texas pear and burrata salad…

In addition to that, American is introducing a wine and chocolate pairing, featuring KHK Wines and K+M Extravirgin Chocolate. Chef Thomas Keller, who co-founded K+M Extravirgin Chocolate with Italian olive oil producer Armando Manni, curated the pairing.

American has launched Flagship Dining, essentially a rebranding and repurposing of the Flagship First Dining facilities. This is being done because American is eliminating “premium” first class in the coming months.

This means American is now offering proper a la carte dining in its business class lounges, increasingly matching the competition. What an awesome change from American! You can find these facilities in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Miami.

What do you make of the evolved Flagship Dining concept? If you visit a Flagship Dining facility, please report back with your experience (food quality, wait times, etc.)!

#6250. Air Canada Cancels 3 Long-Haul Boeing 737 MAX Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Air Canada is a major player in the transatlantic aviation market. The airline maintains an extensive network of flights from Canada to Europe, and earlier this year the airline had three Boeing 737 MAX 8 flights across the pond that were canceled.

As part of Air Canada's network transformation, it is transitioning its fleet of MAX planes to its leisure-focused subsidiary, Air Canada Rouge. This will modernize Rouge's leisure network across North America, the Caribbean, and Central America. This has led the airline to pull back from three transatlantic markets with the type.

With the MAX 8 having the range and capabilities to make nonstop flights from Canada's East Coast to Europe, the airline operated a number of routes with the type to destinations. These included Halifax / Stanfield International Airport (YHZ) to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) to both Edinburgh Airport (EDI) and Nantes (NTE).

With the planes now being allocated elsewhere, these routes will move to the Airbus A321XLR instead, another narrowbody jet operated by the Star Alliance carrier, which is renowned for its long-range capabilities.

For Air Canada, this does not mark the end of the airline serving these city pairs, but instead optimizes its aircraft availability across its fleet. The following table, utilizing data from Cirium, highlights the routes affected by these changes:

Air Canada will continue to operate the 737 MAX on select transatlantic routes next summer, with the airline planning to operate flights from Halifax to Brussels Airport (BRU), Montreal and Toronto to Keflavik International Airport (KEF), and Toronto to Ponta Delgada (PDL).

These changes indicate that a total of just 3.5% of all transatlantic flying for Air Canada will be operated by the MAX 8, down from 6.8% for the third quarter. A total of 329 flights were operated across the pond with this type for Air Canada this quarter alone. Complete data for the same quarters in the last five years below:

Overall, this represents a 43% decrease in transatlantic flights with the MAX between 2026 and 2027.

As Air Canada Rouge prepares to take flight on five new nonstop routes to Europe, passengers can expect a refreshed onboard experience.

Air Canada will continue to transition the MAX 8 to Air Canada Rouge through the end of this year. The first phase of the transition began in March, with the service debuting on routes domestically from Vancouver International Airport (YVR) to Edmonton International Airport (YEG) and Kelowna (YLW).

These planes are configured with 177 seats: 12 Business Class, 18 Preferred Extra Legroom, and 147 standard Economy. Unlike older Rouge planes, these aircraft retain the mainline features, including seatback entertainment, free WiFi for the airline's Aeroplan frequent flyer members, and complimentary beer, wine, and snacks on select routes.

Improvements to the Rouge fleet will cater to customers now enjoying upgraded cabins on shorter trips, with improved technology and enhanced smaller details that make the journey easier and more comfortable.

#6245. Delta Air Lines Cancels 15 Routes From 3 Busiest Hubs: See Full List Now

Network consolidation is inevitable at the best of times, and major carriers like Delta Air Lines are not exempt. External pressures such as high fuel prices have forced airlines to be more clinical than usual with route cuts this year, with the Atlanta-based SkyTeam founding member axing a combined 15 routes from its top three hubs by flights and passengers. These are Atlanta, Detroit, and Minneapolis.

Scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, shows that Atlanta was the top casualty, losing six Delta Air Lines routes. It was followed by Detroit and Minneapolis respectively, with five and four corridors having been shelved between January and October 2026. This does not include routes that operated only briefly to serve special events.

Starting with Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Delta's Michigan hub saw its first cut in May, when flights to Sacramento International Airport (SMF) in California came to an end. This corridor was followed by Reykjavík Keflavík International Airport (KEF) in August and Pensacola and Bozeman in September. None of these routes currently have any Delta flights scheduled in 2027.

Most recently, the airline ended its flights from Detroit to Bangor International Airport in Maine (BGR) in October. Nonetheless, it hasn't been all doom and gloom for Delta in Detroit this year, with the carrier announcing last month that it would be launching a new route from DTW to Athens in June 2027.

Wayne County Airport Authority CEO Chad Newton welcomed the move.

"We appreciate Delta Air Lines’ continued investment in Detroit and are excited about the new opportunities this service will create for tourism, business, and cultural connections."

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) had the biggest share of Delta's route cuts this year, with six corridors falling to the sword. Most of these ended relatively recently, except the route to Santa Barbara Municipal Airport (SBA) in California, which Delta last served in January 2026. Otherwise, the rest were axed in September or October 2026.

Arguably the most interesting of the September cuts was Delta's route from Atlanta to Argyle International Airport (SVD) in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, as it lasted only one season. Elsewhere, September also marked the end of Delta's routes from Atlanta to Rapid City Regional Airport (RAP), Traverse City Cherry Capital Airport (TVC), and Vancouver International Airport (YVR).

Delta's Top Hubs In November 2026 (Cirium)

Meanwhile, Detroit was not the only airport from which Delta ceased flying to Bangor in October 2026. Its route from Atlanta to the Maine city also ended last month. As a result, the carrier now serves only two destinations from Bangor: John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and LaGuardia Airport (LGA). In both cases, flights are operated by Endeavor Air as Delta Connection.

Delta unveils its biggest Delta One overhaul in years, featuring luxury dining, enhanced comfort and global expansion in 2027.

Moving on to Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), the Minnesota hub has lost four of its Delta routes this year. These cuts were split evenly between April and September 2026, with two cuts apiece. In April, the carrier cut its short-haul international leisure network, ceasing service from Minneapolis to St. Maarten in the Caribbean and Mazatlan in Mexico.

Meanwhile, in September, Delta made two more domestic cuts to its Minneapolis network. The routes in question served Williston Basin International Airport (XWA) in North Dakota and Wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina. As a result, Delta now has no flights at all to Williston, while it continues to serve Wilmington from Atlanta with mainline flights and LaGuardia with regional services.

After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane.

The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane.

It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin.

And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes.

United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening —  well ... the outside of it, at least.

As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal.

That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights.

Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK.

While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months.

The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week.

It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service.

Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities.

There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration.

Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar.

The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months.

United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products.

This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets.

American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners.

Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically.

United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years.

So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come.

#6240. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. #6239. Singapore Airlines Unveils New First & Business Class Cabins For A350, 777-9

The wait is finally over — Singapore Airlines has today unveiled its all-new cabins, which were first teased two years ago. Most significantly, this includes a brand new business class, plus the expansion of first class to more planes. This really represents the carrier’s next generation product offering, since these cabins will be installed on future Boeing 777-9s, as well as retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s.

Let’s first talk briefly about which planes will be getting this product, and then we’ll cover the details of the cabins. Keep in mind these changes will also include an updated soft product, including a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins.

Singapore Airlines’ new cabin products will be coming to all of the carrier’s upcoming Boeing 777-9s, as well as to select Airbus A350-900s. This includes a new first class, business class, premium economy, and economy, along with updated inflight entertainment and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

Singapore Airlines has 31 Boeing 777-9s on order, which are expected to eventually be the carrier’s flagship aircraft. These will come delivered with the new cabins. As a matter of fact, Singapore Airlines had initially planned to debut the new cabins on these 777-9s all the way back in 2020. However, delivery of those planes has now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest.

More immediately, Singapore Airlines also plans to invest 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

How will the layouts of A350s change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

With the above out of the way, let’s take a look at Singapore Airlines’ new first class and business class seats. Let me say upfront that:

Below is a chart with the basics of Singapore Airlines’ new first class product.

Singapore Airlines’ new first class seat is designed by PriestmanGoode, and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, and it’ll be available exclusively on Boeing 777-9s and Airbus A350-900ULRS (so not on standard A350-900s, and it won’t be retrofitted on existing aircraft).

Entertainment will be available on a 32″ 4K monitor. As you’d expect, tech will be cutting edge beyond that, with bluetooth audio, wireless, AC, and USB-C charging, etc. There will also be a touchscreen handset that provides easy access to KrisWorld, plus a panel with seat controls and flight information.

One of the nice things is that the center suites have a retractable divider, potentially creating a large, expansive space, so that guests in the center seats can dine and relax together. Singapore Airlines claims that when combined, the double bed becomes the biggest bed in commercial aviation, as it measures 80″ long and 60″ wide.

There won’t be overhead bins in first class, so bags can be stored in a cabin baggage compartment underneath the seat. There will also be a personal wardrobe, and a leather-lined vanity drawer.

What’s my take on Singapore Airlines’ new first class? Quite honestly, this is almost exactly what I was expecting from the airline:

Below is a chart with the basics of Singapore Airlines’ new business class product.

Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat is designed by BMW Designworks, and manufactured by RECARO, and it’ll be available exclusively on Boeing 777-9s and Airbus A350-900s (both long haul and ultra long haul).

Entertainment will be available on a 20-22″ 4K monitor. As you’d expect, tech will be cutting edge beyond that, with bluetooth audio, wireless, AC, and USB-C charging, etc. The airline also highlights how the seat has multiple storage options, which is appreciated.

Perhaps what’s most interesting is how in every other row, the center seats will be very close together, with the ability to form a double bed, which is a feature that customers always appreciate.

What’s my take on Singapore Airlines’ new business class? In some ways it’s what I expected, but there are some real surprises here:

Maybe it’ll look different in person, but am I the only one who is genuinely confused by the color choices? Those yellow accents just feel very… Spirit Airlines or Scoot, no?

When can we expect Singapore Airlines’ new premium products to debut? The expectation is that we’ll see a long haul Airbus A350-900 reconfigured first, and the first of those planes should now enter service in the second quarter of 2027. We don’t yet have any details beyond that.

The expectation is that the first retrofitted A350-900ULR (the ultra long range plane, operating the world’s longest flight) will debut at some point later in 2027, though that’s still up in the air. Meanwhile the 777-9s should start to join the fleet in late 2027 or early 2028 — only time will tell, given never-ending delays with Boeing.

Singapore Airlines should finish retrofitting its 41 A350s with the new cabins by either 2030 or 2031, though that timeline also remains subject to change. The delays with these new products reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines has just unveiled all-new cabins, which includes a new first class and business class. These cabins will be retrofitted on select Airbus A350-900s, and installed on all factory fresh Boeing 777-9s. These new products are long overdue, and I can’t wait to see them in service.

In first class, Singapore Airlines opted for a product that feels on brand, with warm colors, and a functional design that even allows for a double suite in the center seats. Meanwhile in business class, the airline chose a staggered product that looks solid, but I just can’t get over the cabin finishes… maybe it’s just me.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ new long haul cabins?

Some of my takes: -Colours aside, you really have to appreciate how bespoke the product is. Most airlines just chose a seat from a catalogue and apply their own CMF with minimal customization if any. And I like the curvature of the suites. -While First is fine, The finishes in Business Class are generic, like they too what was advertised in the catalogue and just chose the base CMF if that makes sense. Some examples of gorgeous finishes in my opinion would be Cathay's Aria, Emirates, ANA's The Room, Riyadh Air, Hawaiian. While Cathay has shifted from green in business, the new Aria finishes are class and posh. -Apparently only selected aircraft will get the ASTROVA OLED system. My guess would be the NEXT system would be available earlier while the ASTROVA system would have to wait a little longer. And the displays of the A350 will be larger by 2" compared to the 779 is probably due to the size of the suite of the latter. -I would've preferred First to be fully enclosed for a "true" suite. And while leather is not my preference, it does look plush and comfy like you're in a cinema while reclined. Decent overall. nothing revolutionary. And another take, but I predict ANA having an impressive First Class product as it will be akin to a Japanese hotel. I also appreciate how they listed the manufacturer of the seats. And while Cathay doesn't indicate the manufacturer themselves, the fact that we keep guessing just shows you how truly of a bespoke product they have, and that's fine too! I also foresee a refurbishment for their medium-haul product in a few years.

#6238. Allegiant Air Cancels Massive 25 Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

One of America's largest ultra-low-cost carriers has cut a massive 25 routes from its winter schedule. This comes as Allegiant Air reevaluates seasonal routes and ponders the return of those flights next year.

Three that last served in November last year will not operate this month, while January through August 2026 continue to see route cuts as the airline adjusts its schedule. Cirium data analyzed by Simple Flying shows many routes have been cut, and some airports are no longer served. A number of these services will now only operate across the summer.

Las Vegas-based Allegiant Air is a US budget airline that offers no-frills, nonstop flying to destinations across the United States. The carrier has no international service and solely relies on the domestic US market. With a fleet of more than 120 aircraft, these are mixed between the Airbus A319, A320 and Boeing 737 MAX 7 and MAX 8-200.

Reviewing historical flight schedules for 2025 and 2026, and comparing them to this winter's schedule, the airline has shaved 25 routes in total, with November seeing three routes absent from its network, including Myrtle Beach (MYR) to Niagara Falls (IAG), Phoenix (PHX) to Asheville (AVL), and Sarasota (SRQ) to Portsmouth (PSM).

The cuts don't stop there; Bellingham (BLI) to Los Angeles (LAX), Nashville (BNA) to Peoria (PIA), Cincinnati (CVG) to Los Angeles, and Las Vegas (LAS) to Boise (BOI) have disappeared for this coming January. This marks the airline's full withdrawal from Los Angeles International Airport. The full list of route cuts for November 2025 to January 2026 is detailed in the table below:

Emphasizing that a number of these routes will continue to operate seasonally in the busier summer months, the airline's overall decline for winter routes saw the airline trim two additional services in April and eight in May. Including the airlines ultimate withdrawal from San Francisco's Oakland International Airport (OAK) airport.

For April 2026, terminated routes include Fort Lauderdale (FLL) to Traverse City (TVC), and Orlando/Sanford (SFB) to Columbia (CAE).

Comparing May 2026, routes no longer scheduled include Bellingham to Oakland (OAK), Bellingham to Palm Springs (PSP), Fort Lauderdale to Columbia, Fort Lauderdale to Huntington (HTS), Fort Lauderdale to Savannah (SAV), Las Vegas to Chattanooga (CHA), Punta Gorda (PGD) to New Orleans (MSY), and Phoenix (PHX) to Pittsburgh (PIT). A complete list is in the table below:

In these numbers, Fort Lauderdale has lost three nonstop services since earlier this year, whereas Bellingham, a longtime Allegiant base, was closed and saw the loss of two West Coast routes.

Seasonal demand and leisure-first strategy prompt aircraft redeployment, reshaping connections and leaving gaps in service.

The airline hasn't stopped there; although these routes are in the Northern Hemisphere summer season, they are currently not scheduled to operate in 2027. August route cuts include Asheville (AVL) to Chicago Midway (MDW), Bellingham to Burbank (BUR), Nashville to Akron/Canton (CAK), Washington Dulles (IAD) to Savannah, Jacksonville (JAX) to Des Moines (DSM), Las Vegas to Lexington (LEX), Portland (PDX) to Idaho Falls (IDA), and Sarasota (SRQ) to Nashville.

Across this analysis, the airline has clearly cut a number of routes that have historically operated from major hub airports, which usually carry high landing and operating costs, instead pivoting operations to regional alternatives. This helps the airline turn a profit on low fares that require low operational costs and high aircraft utilization.

#6236. American Airlines Adds New App Option When Flights Go Wrong—Try For An Earlier Flight Without Giving Up Your Confirmed Seat

American Airlines is making it easier to try for an earlier flight when your travel falls apart. Its app and website will now offer standby options when you’re dealing with a travel disruption while keeping your new confirmed flight. You don’t need an agent for this – it’s part of their self-service tool. The change to list yourself for free standby on an earlier flight went into effect this week. During a disruption, the flight you can confirm may be hours later than one you could actually get on if a seat opens up. You no longer need to deal with customer service to get on the standby list. . How The New Standby Option Works American calls its tool Dynamic Rebooking. Here’s the sequence described in an internal company memo: Open your disrupted trip on aa.com or in the American Airlines app. Start with Flight Options or Rebook Trip in the disruption banner. If your flight was canceled and you don’t have a replacement, confirm one first. Choose a flight with availability, then return to Flight Options to look for standby. Look for earlier nonstop flights. Up to three standby options may appear when American can’t confirm the earlier rebooking. Pick one. You can join one standby list at a time through this tool. You can remove yourself or switch to another option without contacting an employee. Keep your confirmed flight while you wait. Your itinerary changes only if you clear onto the standby flight. If you’re confirmed for an 8 p.m. flight and the app can’t confirm you on the 5 p.m., you can standby for it while remaining confirmed on that 8 p.m.. If you don’t clear, your confirmed itinerary remains intact. Employees are told, Do not cancel the customer’s confirmed flight because the customer joined standby If you do clear standby you lose the confirmation on your original flight so if you can’t make it you need to remove yourself from standby. What American Is Actually Adding For Passengers American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process. Here’s one example of where this matters: an Executive Platinum member facing a seven hour Dallas–Charlotte delay could see confirmed alternatives in the disruption tool, but couldn’t find a way to request earlier standby. Even accepting a later confirmed flight didn’t solve it. An agent eventually added them to standby and they cleared. I covered American’s new disruption banners in January, alongside rebooking, baggage tracking, and digital hotel and meal vouchers. Standby was one of the additions they said was coming. American also described the feature in its October 26 iPhone app release notes. American is trying to offer more tools for managing disruptions. That’s both a cost savings and also empowering to the passenger. A customer who feels in control of their options is going to have a better view of the airline than one who feels at the mercy of broader forces. It’s about raising net promoter scores when things go wrong, which is part of customers being willing to be repeat purchasers, purchasers of premium products, and passengers willing to pay more to fly American. That’s the strategy anyway. In contrast, in 2024, American restricted most passengers to digital standby even when its systems couldn’t handle their requests. They restored agent assistance in July 2025. Improving digital tools and offering agent help is ultimately the right direction to be moving. The Limits Customers Should Know Nothing is being taken away here, but the new tool has limits: Three displayed choices means one standby request. You aren’t joining three lists at once, and the memo only describes nonstop options. That’s not every possible way to get where you’re going. This doesn’t fix ordinary same day confirmed changes. I’ve written about American’s restrictive availability and routing rules. This update is an improvement for recovery from disruptions, but ordinary standby and confirmed flight changes are still broken at American. United introduced a broader version of this in September: disrupted customers can select up to three eligible earlier flights, and United monitors for seats and texts when one opens. Customers choose whether to switch while retaining their confirmed reservation until they decide. American’s memo allows one standby listing and says the confirmed itinerary changes when standby clears. This isn’t going to change the need for me to work with an agent, but it’s going to be helpful to a lot of people. Plus, American’s Executive Platinum members and higher can have more than one flight in their itinerary confirmed at a time during irregular operations (for instance, I book a backup in case I misconnect when my first segment is delayed – rather than having to make the call early to make the switch and give up my shot at making it, I can lock in the option of flying later while still running for my connection). And bear in mind that you can still ask for a partner flight (such as on Alaska Airlines) if your confirmed option is the next day as well. (1) As an hypothetical executive, I might think, this app change the need for agents to work with customers. Therefore, lets streamline the customer service personal. American would not do that would they? (2) Why is an earlier standby flight available? I have switched to earlier flights, but they ended up being delayed past my original flight. I’m pretty skeptical about AA’s IT for passengers. The week before last they did a pretty lousy job dealing with their problems. I was flying home from LAS with a connection in DFW. First flight was delayed repeatedly. The app kept promising to rebook me if my connection became non viable. By the time we boarded in Vegas my connection – with a change of terminals – was seven minutes. The app still did nothing so I switched flights myself. Then the flight out of DFW was severely delayed. Ended up home very late only to discover that my bag was mishandled and was still in Dallas. AA’s IT didn’t bother informing me until I was the last person at the baggage carousel at almost two in the morning.

That experience made me incredibly angry and gave me no confidence whatsoever in the technology that American is using.

@Christian — Yikes. Did you at least receive a perfunctory automated “sorry” after that ordeal? I mean, I know, like, actually receiving your checked bag(s) timely would’ve been preferred, and if not, reliable communication and reimbursement, but, you know, the ‘free’ market and lifting bootstraps is the best we can do for now… *facepalm* (this is why I try to do carry-on only.)

As recently as last week, the poor IT underpinnings of AA’s app effectively prevented its use even for confirming later rebookings. GAs and FAs are being told to tell disrupted passengers to rebook in the app rather than call or line up, only for the pax who listen to find themselves last in the queue when the app fails,

I’d prefer to see AA focus on getting the existing functionality working before they add new capabilities

@Frequent Delay Victim — There’s little incentive for AA or any major US carrier to properly invest in operational reliability because there’s no real financial penalty for them failing to deliver for you. (Oh, you’ll go to a competitor? Well, turns out, AA’s the only one operating that nonstop; oh, and Delta, United, Southwest, etc., also frequently delay and cancel with no real recourse other than a partial refund or expiring extremely limited silly credit.) We need major reforms that include actual consumer protections, or this will just keep getting worse and worse.

I think this is helpful, but I wonder if the alternatives offered are only valid for the original departing airport? In NY, LA, SFO and other airports I would not mind going to a different airport to catch an earlier flight, time permitting. But to date, alternatives have only been offered for the same airport you were originally booked from. Equally, I don’t NEED to get an alternative for LGA if I can catch an earlier option to JFK or EWR. Same for other destinations. I am sure AI could figure this out 😉

#6235. World of Hyatt Card Limited Time Bonus Offer: Earn Four Free Night Awards

We’ve just seen a new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the World of Hyatt Credit Card, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d consider this to be one of the most lucrative hotel credit cards out there — it’s a product you don’t get just for the bonus, but instead, for the long term value that it offers.

Let’s take a look at the details of the card bonus and eligibility requirements, as well as the long term value.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card bonus offer

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome bonus that consists of four Category 1-4 free night awards after spending $5,000 within the first three months.

World of Hyatt Category 4 properties retail for up to 25,000 points per night, so the absolute maximum value of this offer is 100,000 points. However, I of course wouldn’t value it that highly. That’s because these free night awards expire 12 months after they’re issued, and you also can’t top off these awards to redeem at more expensive properties. So actually maxing out the value of these isn’t easy.

One thing I should mention is that while I don’t love the lack of flexibility of this welcome offer, it’s significantly better than the standard bonus, which tends to be lackluster. Obviously Chase and Hyatt know that this is a card people will get for the long term value, rather than just for the bonus.

For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.

If you’re interested in applying for the World of Hyatt Credit Card, the eligibility rules for the bonus are pretty straightforward. This product is available to you if you don’t have this exact card, and haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months.

So that means you could potentially earn the bonus if you’ve had the card in the past. Furthermore, eligibility is unrelated to whether you have the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more).

On top of that, Chase’s general application rules apply, including that you can typically be approved for at most two Chase cards every 30 days, and the Chase 5/24 rule is also worth considering (you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to be approved for this card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The World of Hyatt Card is one that offers a lot of long term value, so only think of the welcome bonus as being part of the bigger picture. The World of Hyatt Card has a $95 annual fee, and offers the following perks, among other things:

This is a card I’ve had for years, and one that I spend at least $15,000 on annually, so that I earn the second free night award, plus six additional elite nights. If you stay at Hyatts with any frequency, having this card should be a no-brainer. For more details, read my full World of Hyatt Card review.

If you’re looking for a Hyatt co-branded credit card but want a business card instead, then the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card is for you. The card is currently offering a bonus of 70,000 points after spending $7,000 within the first three months.

At my valuation of 1.4 cents per point, that’s roughly $980 in value, which more than offsets the $199 annual fee in year one.

Eligibility is straightforward, as you can’t currently hold this specific card, and you can’t have received a welcome bonus on it within the past 24 months. Having the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card doesn’t affect your eligibility, as you can hold both cards and earn bonuses on each. Standard Chase application rules apply.

For more details, read my World of Hyatt Business Card review, as well as my World of Hyatt personal vs. business card comparison.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome offer that can earn you four Category 1-4 free night awards upon completing minimum spending. Category 4 properties go for up to 25,000 points per night, so this is potentially quite a substantial welcome bonus.

However, the bonus isn’t the main reason you get this card. Instead, it’s about the long term value proposition, including elite nights toward status, an anniversary free night award, etc. Furthermore, it’s a card that’s worth spending $15,000 on per year, if you can swing it, so you can earn a second free night award and six more elite nights toward status.

If this card has been on your radar, this is a good time to apply…

I’ve held the (see rates and fees) for eight years, and despite carrying more than 25 credit cards, it’s one I’ll continue renewing year after year.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Between an annual free night, automatic elite status and the ability to earn valuable Hyatt points on spending, I consistently receive far more value than the card’s affordable $95 annual fee.

It isn’t the right fit for everyone. Hyatt has a much smaller global footprint than Marriott, Hilton and IHG, so travelers who rarely stay at Hyatt hotels may be better served by a more flexible travel rewards card. However, if Hyatt is already part of your travel plans — or you’d like it to become one — the World of Hyatt card is one of the best mid-tier hotel cards on the market. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you’re comparing several hotel credit cards, here’s what you need to know at a glance:

Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. Since Hyatt prices these properties between 3,000 and 25,000 points per night, there’s plenty of opportunity to extract well over $95 in value. Free nights expire 12 months after issuance.

I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

Simply holding the card gives you complimentary Discoverist status.

While Discoverist isn’t Hyatt’s most rewarding elite tier, I still appreciate benefits like preferred room upgrades and late checkout (when available) and a 10% bonus on eligible Hyatt spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

I’ve found those elite night credits incredibly valuable. By combining the five annual elite nights from the card with my Hyatt stays and strategic spending to earn an additional six nights, I qualified for top-tier Globalist status in August 2025, which I’ll enjoy through February 2027.

Related: Was going all-in on Hyatt Globalist worth it? My honest take

Chase issues this card, so you'll receive several useful travel protections, including:

These protections aren't as extensive as those you'd receive with a premium travel card, but that's to be expected given this card's modest annual fee.

Related: Is the World of Hyatt credit card worth the annual fee?

One of my favorite things about the World of Hyatt program is that earning and redeeming points is refreshingly straightforward.

Unlike most major hotel loyalty programs, Hyatt still publishes an award chart, making award pricing more predictable.

When you stay at Hyatt hotels, these earnings stack with the points you earn as a World of Hyatt member. Since cardholders receive complimentary Discoverist status, you’ll also earn a 10% bonus on your base points, meaning you can earn up to 9.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Hyatt purchases. That represents a solid 16% return on Hyatt purchases, per our November 2026 valuations.

I generally use this card for Hyatt stays and tax payments that help me reach the $15,000 annual threshold for the second free night certificate.

Otherwise, I typically use my  (see rates and fees) for most travel and dining purchases, then transfer those Chase Ultimate Rewards points to my Hyatt account whenever I need to top up my balance for an award stay.

That gives me the best of both worlds: I earn more rewards on everyday travel and dining while keeping my points flexible until I’m ready to book. If I don’t end up needing Hyatt points, I can always transfer them to one of Chase’s 13 other airline or hotel partners instead.

Related: 6 of the best credit cards for travel purchases — beyond flights and hotels

In my opinion, Hyatt points remain among the most valuable hotel points due to their flexibility.

Award nights start at just 3,000 points for a Category 1 property at the Lowest rate and range up to 75,000 points for a top-tier Category 8 property under Hyatt’s five-tier standard award chart.

I’ve used Hyatt points for everything from inexpensive city breaks to luxury resorts. Some of my favorite redemptions include:

Hyatt also lets you redeem points for Points + Cash stays, suite upgrades, club lounge access and Find experiences. While those options can make sense occasionally, I almost always get the best value by redeeming points for standard award nights.

Related: 22 best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

Despite being one of my favorite hotel credit cards, the won’t be the right fit for every traveler.

The biggest drawback is Hyatt’s relatively small footprint. While Hyatt has more than 1,500 hotels and all-inclusive properties across 80-plus countries, that’s still far fewer than Marriott or Hilton. If you frequently travel to destinations without a Hyatt, you may struggle to maximize the card’s benefits.

Those who prioritize earning the highest possible rewards on everyday spending will likely find better options elsewhere. Beyond Hyatt purchases and spending toward the $15,000 threshold for a second free night certificate, this card isn’t particularly rewarding for dining, travel or everyday purchases.

Finally, travelers looking for premium perks like airport lounge access, annual travel credits and luxury benefits across multiple hotel brands should consider a premium travel rewards card instead.

For most travelers, I think the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is the better choice than the (see rates and fees).

Both cards help you earn Hyatt points and elite status, but the business version is designed primarily for business owners. It offers bonus categories geared toward business spending and additional benefits for companies, while the personal card provides better long-term value for most travelers, thanks to its annual Category 1-4 free night certificate.

By comparison, I think the World of Hyatt Business card's $199 annual fee is harder to justify year after year because it lacks an anniversary free night. It does offer up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year, but that requires Hyatt spending and there's no way to get outsized value like you might with a free night.

Unless you own a business and can maximize the business-specific earning categories, I’d start with the personal card.

Someone who uses all four free night certificates at the highest-priced properties would save up to 100,000 World of Hyatt points, making this offer worth up to $1,650 (based on TPG valuations).

This is a very strong bonus compared to other historical welcome offers, though not the absolute all-time highest offer for new cardmembers. The best-ever welcome offer included five free-night awards (offer no longer available). Having said that, if you max out the four certificates, this would be considered the most lucrative offer since February.

Despite being a great offer right now, some travelers may prefer to wait until the introductory bonus is awarded in points instead. Unlike free nights, there are no hotel category restrictions for redeeming points. The expiration date for free nights is also stricter.

I’ve carried the World of Hyatt Credit Card for eight years, and it’s one of the few hotel credit cards I have no intention of canceling.

The annual Category 1-4 free night certificate has consistently offset the card’s $95 annual fee, while the elite night credits helped me qualify for Globalist status last year. Add in Hyatt’s strong redemption value, and it’s easy to see why this remains my favorite mid-tier hotel credit card.

If you regularly stay at Hyatt properties, I think the World of Hyatt card deserves a place in your wallet. If you rarely stay with Hyatt, though, you’ll probably get more long-term value from a flexible travel rewards card.
