#6214. Flights In Europe Face Endless Bomb Threats: “This Is Only The Beginning”

It has been a rather rough week for many airlines in Europe, as dozens of flights have been diverted, canceled, or delayed, due to bomb threats. There’s obviously some sort of a coordinated effort here, but it’s hard to know what exactly is going on, beyond just the desire to create chaos (thanks to 1990_ for flagging this)…

The concept of bomb threats being called in on flights is nothing new. Sometimes people are dumb enough to call in a bomb threat because they’re running late for a flight, and think that’s the best way not to miss it. Other times people will call in bomb threats as a prank.

Rarely is a bomb threat actually called in on a flight where there’s a bomb. That comes down to two reasons — it’s exceedingly rare for flights to be bombed (thank goodness), and if someone actually wants to take down a plane, they wouldn’t issue a warning, since that kind of defeats the purpose.

So that brings us to what has gone on in Europe this week, particularly on Tuesday, Thursday, and again today (Friday). Dozens of flights across airlines have had bomb threats called in on them, and airlines generally have to take these seriously. This has now happened to over 50 flights, departing from roughly a dozen countries.

In some cases the bomb threats were called in before takeoff, so passengers could be deplaned, allowing a search to happen before departure. In other cases, the threats came in mid-flight, leading to diversions, and even fighter jet escorts, in some situations.

In no case were any credible threats found, though. It goes without saying that this is incredibly frustrating for all parties. This is a massive waste of time and resources, given that these kinds of threats are consistently fake. At the same time, governments and airlines have to take these threats seriously, because imagine what would happen if a threat were proven to be real, and it was ignored (personally I think they should just be ignored, but that’s neither here nor there).

It’s not known for sure who is behind this attack, or just how centrally coordinated it is, rather than there being a copycat element to this.

Some emails taking credit for these attacks were signed as being from “the fighters of the Male State,” referencing a Russian far right, ultra nationalist movement that was founded in 2016. However, in a Telegram post today, the group’s founder denied involvement in this, and said the group hasn’t even existed since 2021.

Another email sent to media outlets regarding these attacks said that “this is only the beginning,” and threatened further attacks (or at least threats of attacks) across European transport.

The timing of this is likely not a coincidence, as Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky is currently visiting Europe for a series of meetings regarding the war with Russia.

It goes without saying that this could get messy. If this is really coming out of Russia, it’ll be hard for European authorities to hold them accountable. And it’s also easy enough for the culprits to try to mask where their threats come from.

If the threats keep coming, then one wonders how this will be handled — will this all just continue, or will the threats be ignored at some point?

Dozens of flights across Europe have been impacted by bomb threats this week, which is obviously incredibly frustrating. None were found to be credible, but they’ve all been taken seriously, with everything from aircraft evacuations, to diversions, to fighter jet escorts.

It can be hard to track down the source of these threats, especially if it’s some tech-savvy, foreign operation. An email claiming to be associated with the group behind these threats suggest that this is only the beginning. Only time will tell how this plays out, because if the threats continue and authorities have no way to take action against the foreign culprits, their options might be limited.

What do you make of this Europe airplane bomb threat situation?

#6212. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6211. U.S. Airlines Face New Collusion Lawsuits-Sharing Data To Keep Ticket Prices High

Airfares rose 22.4% over the past year, according to the government’s September inflation report. And American Airlines, Delta, United other major carriers are accused of using shared airfare and customer shopping data to keep ticket prices high. Two new class action lawsuits say the airlines have built a way to spot competitors’ discounts and discourage the price cutting that could save passengers money. There’s a plausible antitrust claim here. There’s also a straightforward explanation for much of the same activity: airlines need to know when they’re charging more than competitors so they can lower their prices. The kind of information sharing that’s happening does not – on its own – amount to a legal violation. I just wrote about former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker explaining how airlines use Wall Street analysts to pressure competitors to stop growing, even while denying that executives signal each other. These lawsuits raise a related question about the systems pricing departments use every day: whether airlines have agreed to share information in a way that helps them avoid competing. Cory Garner flags two new complaints: Ward v. ATPCO, filed in federal court in Seattle, and Brown v. ATPCO, filed in Virginia. Between them, they name American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, Southwest Airlines, Alaska, Hawaiian and JetBlue, along with the Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its 3Victors subsidiary. ATPCO is owned by airlines and has long distributed fares and fare rules. These cases target its newer shopping data business. Airlines increasingly generate offers that vary by channel, itinerary, bundle and customer. Those offers can be harder for competitors to observe than a published fare. Iris collects shopping data. Airlines and other participants contribute information and receive competitive information in return. PriceEye makes offers easier to compare. It supplies competitive data and alerts that draw attention to differences in pricing. DemandView identifies demand before it becomes bookings. Search activity can show where customers want to travel even when they haven’t bought tickets. 3Victors describes the information exchange as “the more you contribute, the more you receive.” And it says Iris collects all the offers returned by a shopping request, including different brands, cabins and prices which is more than an airline would get scraping a limited website search result. The lawsuits argue this gives competitors visibility into competitor pricing they wouldn’t otherwise have, including for offers that haven’t resulted in sales. An airline that might discount to fill seats instead knows rivals can quickly discover and respond to the offer, so they do not make it. If an airline expects every price cut to be matched almost immediately, it may see less opportunity to win business by cutting in the first place. The same information can make tickets cheaper. If an airline is selling a flight for $100 more than a competitor, getting an alert that they’re being underpriced lets them adjust their fares to avoid losing a sale. And better demand information can support an extra flight or a larger aircraft, adding seat supply which supports lower fares. As I’ve explained when American, United and Southwest all showed the same $523 fare, independently responding to a rival’s price isn’t an antitrust violation. Similar prices aren’t enough to establish an agreement. An airline can generally observe a publicly available price and decide to match it. Competitors agreeing to keep prices above a certain level is price fixing. An agreement to exchange sensitive information that makes competition less vigorous is somewhere in beteween – it’s alleged here that the agreement violates the Sherman Act by unreasonably restraining competition. The lawsuit itself doesn’t establish that happens – they need to get to the discovery stage and come up with something juicy. In United States v. Container Corp., the Supreme Court found reciprocal exchange of recent customer-specific prices even without an agreement to adhere to a price schedule to violate the law. On the other hand, the Court also recognized that information exchanges can improve competition. Garner points out that the old government case against ATPCO involved airlines circulating proposed fares before customers could buy them. Airlines could see whether competitors would go along with an increase before exposing themselves to losing sales. PriceEye’s ability to show current offers for future flights isn’t the same thing. A price you can buy today for travel next June isn’t advance notice of a planned price increase. I’m skeptical that what the airlines are doing here actually breaks the law. At a minimum, their defenses are pretty good. A faster, more reliable way to observe bookable fares can help airlines compete. These systems don’t make pricing decisions. There’s no common agent fixing fares. Higher fares alone don’t show this system caused them. Fuel prices and resulting capacity discipline have mattered a lot. Meanwhile, airfares have actually been falling in inflation adjusted terms and even with the recent run-up are lower than they were pre-pandemic. Assuming the cases make it through to discovery, actual contracts airlines signed and feeds will show agreements and the real data being shared, as well as how the services are marketed and discussed at the airlines. If the case goes very far, I’d imagine we’d see a settlement involving money and tighter limits on data sharing to avoid triple damages plus fees. #6210. Singapore Airlines’ New Business Class Finishes Look Cheap, Mismatched

Earlier I covered how Singapore Airlines unveiled its new first & business class, which should enter service in 2027 (hopefully). These products look like very nice improvements over the existing cabins, even if they’re not revolutionary.

That being said, I have to give Singapore Airlines some tough love on the new business class seats. Let me acknowledge that I’m a huge fan of Singapore Airlines as a brand. Any list I keep of the best airlines in the world (whether it’s the best airline brand, best first class, best business class, best inflight service, best inflight entertainment, etc.) has Singapore Airlines on it… that’s how highly I think of the brand!

But I’m also honest, regardless of how it fits my preconceived notions of a brand. I feel like I’m saying what everyone else is thinking, seemingly except for most influencers who are in Singapore for the launch event, who are just casually glossing over this… so much for attention to detail!

When I think of Singapore Airlines, the first thing that comes to mind for me is how deliberate the airline is. I don’t think there’s an airline that’s more intentional with every aspect of its guest experience, from the tone of voice with which staff speak, to warm and elegant design.

I’d say Singapore Airlines’ new first class actually looks really on brand. It’s a nice evolution of what the carrier has historically offered — it’s warm and elegant without being outdated.

And then you move to business class, and it looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby. The gray and black is generic, the yellow accents look cheap, and then there’s so much going on with the blue and white bulkheads (if that’s actually how they’ll look).

And the Scoot reference isn’t even sarcastic. For those not familiar, Scoot is Singapore Airlines’ low cost carrier, and look at the seat finishes you’ll find there!

Usually there’s some consistency between seat finishes and wider branding, including the livery, flight attendant uniforms, etc. In this case, it’s not only not aligned, but they seem at odds with one another. There’s otherwise not a hint of yellow (or neon green, or whatever that is) in Singapore Airlines’ branding.

What so bizarre to me is how the first and business class finishes are completely mismatched, and you wouldn’t assume they belonged to the same airline. That’s because Singapore Airlines worked with different design firms (separate from the seating manufacturers as such) for the two cabins.

BMW Designworks was behind the business class seats, while PriestmanGoode was behind the first class seats. I think it’s safe to say there was no coordination between the two. I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic.

It’s clear that Singapore Airlines put many years of effort into this product, and frankly I’m just surprised that Singapore Airlines executives signed off on this. Am I just in the minority in thinking this isn’t a good look for the airline? Did some marketer assure Singapore Airlines executives this was great branding, and they were wrong? Or did everyone just independently decide that this looks great?

If they at least eliminated the yellow stripes, it would no longer look cheap, but would instead look generic. I’m just surprised that this is the conclusion they came to.

Singapore Airlines of course had a big media event in Singapore to celebrate the launch of this product. I don’t attend media events, just as a general policy, because I don’t find them to be a great use of time. But I certainly do enjoy seeing the coverage from others.

What I find fascinating is the inherent bias that exists when someone is invited to something. For example, if you look at the comments on my post about the new cabins, the single thing most commented on by OMAAT community members is how bad the business class colors look.

If you watched the videos on social media about this, there’s oddly no commentary on that. Admittedly I haven’t seen all the coverage, but the worst coverage I’ve seen is someone saying they “don’t mind” the colors, and that it’s a “big departure” from the old look. Okay, that’s not exactly an endorsement.

I also haven’t found a single person who attended the event who said “I love the new colors,” which probably tells you everything you need to know. For that matter, it’s one thing if people acknowledged “I realize the colors might not look good in pictures, but in person, it’s a different story.” But I haven’t heard that either.

To me this gets at the rather complicated relationship between so many brands and influencer types. If you can say all the things you love about the product, shouldn’t you also feel totally comfortable criticizing the parts of the experience you don’t like, though?

While we’re on this topic, let me add one more point. Being able to sit in seats at media events like this is of course cool, but it really doesn’t actually give you an impression of what it’s like to fly in a product, and that’s why it’s not something I particularly value, as an experience.

Of course a big business class seat is comfortable when you sit in it for a minute, and you’re filming content. But the real test of a product is when you spend hours in the seat, when you recline the seat into a bed, when you try to move your laptop around while you’re being served a meal, etc.

I once had the opportunity to spend a night in an aircraft seat on the ground (I can’t really say more, since I signed an NDA, but it was to provide feedback to a seating manufacturer). To me that was fascinating, because it really gives you an understanding of what the experience is like. My feeling about the seat was very different after being in the seat for many hours vs. when I sat down.

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its new cabins, and there’s a lot to be excited about, as the hard products look very nice. However, Singapore Airlines’ new business class cabin finishes are a real mystery to me, because the yellow stripe looks cheap (I mean, it seems to be inspired by the carrier’s low cost subsidiary), and completely mismatched with first class.

The airline used different design firms for first class and business class. For an airline so focused on attention to detail and being very deliberate in terms of design, this strikes me as a misstep. Anyway, Singapore Airlines, I still love you and think you’re one of the best airlines in the world…

Where do you stand on Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat finishes? Does anyone love them?

#6208. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6206. U.S. Now Requires Ebola Attestation For Flights From Abroad — How To Complete It And Who Can Be Denied Boarding

Flying to the U.S. from abroad now requires an Ebola attestation. You have to confirm that you haven’t been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the previous 21 days before boarding your flight even if you’ve never been anywhere near Africa. An internal American Airlines memo explains how they’re collecting it, including what happens when a kiosk sends you to your phone and what to do if you can’t use the app. For most passengers, this is another check-in step. For someone who’s recently been to Congo, it can mean being unable to board a flight home even with a U.S. passport. Who Has To Complete An Ebola Attestation? The federal requirement took effect for flights departing for the United States at or after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 3, 2026. It applies across airlines, including foreign airlines. You provide a declaration about recent travel history. That’s it – there’s no Ebola test or vaccination certificate. U.S. citizens, foreign visitors and green card holders are covered. Passengers merely connecting through the United States are covered, too. Departures from airports with U.S. immigration preclearance still count. Domestic flights aren’t covered. U.S. territories aren’t foreign countries under this rule, so a nonstop flight from Puerto Rico to the mainland doesn’t trigger it. The form requires an attestation for each individual, including children. A parent or another authorized representative can complete it for a child or someone unable to do it themselves. The current order runs through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on December 18, 2026. The March 31, 2027 date printed on the form is the expiration of its paperwork approval, not the scheduled end of the travel requirement. How To Complete It On American Airlines American’s October 30 internal advisory lays out the airport procedures. Use the app or aa.com during check-in. The app requires you to complete the attestation before you can finish checking in. Once submitted, American adds a completion marker to your reservation. Don’t expect the kiosk to collect it. American says kiosks don’t support attestation collection. They’ll display a QR code directing you to the mobile app, and you’ll need to finish the attestation before completing kiosk check-in. No working phone? Ask for paper. American allows passengers to bring a completed paper form or request one at the airport. You can download the official fillable form here. An agent can also record a verbal attestation. You must first review the attestation wording. The agent then asks you to confirm your travel history and records that you reviewed the language and attested. Both American’s memo and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s instructions permit this. For paper, enter the name, select the appropriate option for yourself or someone you’re authorized to represent, and sign and date it. Read both pages and give the completed form to the airline. American must retain completed paper attestations for 42 days. If the app won’t let you proceed, ask an agent to check whether the attestation is recorded. American calls the completion marker ADOC. Ideally complete this before heading to the airport. If the technology fails, ask for the paper form. If You’ve Been To Congo, The Form Can Stop Your Trip The question is whether you’ve been physically present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, not whether you feel healthy or believe you were exposed. Even a connection at a Congolese airport counts, including a stop where you stayed on the aircraft. The State Department confirms that U.S. citizens are also barred from boarding commercial flights to the United States during the waiting period. Limited government exemptions exist, including authorized medical transport and limited humanitarian cases. The calendar calculation is easy to mess up: Day 0: The day you leave Congo. Days 1–21: The full calendar days you remain outside the country. Day 22: The first day you can board a flight to the United States, assuming you meet other entry requirements. Leave Congo on November 1, for instance, and the first eligible boarding date is November 23. The CDC illustrates the waiting period this way: Uganda and South Sudan have separate rules. Under the current entry restrictions, non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. nationals, including green card holders, who’ve recently been in either country must also wait outside the United States. U.S. citizens and nationals who’ve been there, but not Congo, can return through New York JFK, Washington Dulles or Atlanta for public health screening. Airport connections count for these rules as well. How Serious Is The Ebola Outbreak? The CDC’s November 3 update, reporting data through November 1 lists 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 confirmed deaths almost all in Congo which is the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded. Outbreak Cases Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic About 28,600 reported About 11,300 2018–2020 Congo outbreak 3,470 reported 2,287 2026 outbreak, through November 1 10,563 confirmed 5,130 confirmed he current outbreak also passed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation; the 2018 outbreak took about 235 days. Conflict, weak health services and difficulty tracing contacts have helped it spread. Kenya and Nigeria reported imported cases in October. Ebola is extremely serious if you become infected, but the risk of becoming infected is low. The CDC reports no U.S. cases associated with this outbreak and considers introduction into the United States very unlikely. (But they aren’t always right about these things…) Ebola spreads through infected blood and other body fluids. It’s not airborne and it isn’t believed to spread by pre-symptomatic people. Taking a flight with someone exposed to Ebola isn’t going to get you sick. You need exposure to their fluids. Then illness can progress from fever, aches and fatigue to severe vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration and organ failure. The outbreak’s reported fatality rate has been around half (but probably overstates things because those dying of Ebola wind up as identified cases, while many who don’t die likely to do not). When 2021 Ebola travel restrictions were put in place, there were approved vaccines and antibody treatments. Those were for the Zaire type of Ebola while this is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there’s no approved vaccine or specific treatment. How Much Will The Attestation Help? Ebola can take up to 21 days to cause symptoms. Someone can be infected, feel well and pass a temperature check while still incubating the disease. Waiting after leaving the outbreak country gives that infection time to become apparent before a U.S. flight. During the earlier epidemic, about 38,000 travelers received enhanced assessments at U.S. ports of entry. One was later diagnosed with Ebola who had no symptoms when he arrived and reported his illness afterward. A declaration’s effectiveness depends on truthful reporting. Requiring three weeks of extra time outside the United States creates an incentive for untruthful reporting. What To Do If You’re Restricted From Flying If you’re barred because of recent travel to an affected country, the Transportation Department’s October 28 enforcement notice preserves passenger protections: For a communicable-disease travel refusal, the passenger can choose qualifying rebooking within 90 days without penalty at the original applicable fare, or a refund for unused flights. A required significant itinerary change, such as rerouting for health screening, triggers a refund if you decline the changed trip. The separate public health travel restriction rules provide transferable credits valid for at least five years. You select the applicable refund or credit remedy, rather than collect both. If you’re refused travel on this basis, get it in writing. The airline must provide that explanation within 10 days of your request. #6204. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6203. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

#6201. New Federal Reserve Research Finds Cutting Merchant Swipe Fees Even Hurts Consumers Who Don’t Earn Rewards

You can earn no miles, no points and no cash back from your credit card and still lose if the government cuts credit card merchant swipe fees. Research from two Philadelphia Federal Reserve economists explains why: the money banks collect when you spend helps pay for better borrowing terms. That’s a problem for the retailers’ argument that consumers who don’t collect rewards are simply paying for everyone else’s vacations. I wrote this week about why the legislation threatening card rewards isn’t dead, even with Dick Durbin retiring and Roger Marshall losing his Senate seat. The political sales pitch is that reducing merchants’ payment costs saves consumers money. That isn’t true and has never been true anywhere in the world it’s been tried. It’s cover for retailers who want the benefits of accepting credit cards, but think the government should require the service be offered to them for less money. But credit cards aren’t just a convenient way to make purchases. They also provide financing for those purchases, and the merchant fee helps support that. Even A Card With No Rewards Can Give Something Back Satyajit Chatterjee and Burcu Eyigungor’s Credit Effects of Credit Card Interchange Fees uses bank supervisory data to examine an overlooked part of the debate: what interchange does to credit itself. The June 26 paper was highlighted in a new Bank of Japan summary. In the data, rewards cards have higher credit limits. Cards without rewards have lower interest rates despite higher default rates. They argue that rewards make repayment more attractive because default means losing access to future rewards. And when a bank keeps interchange instead of paying rewards, competition encourages it to offer better rates and limits to attract the customer’s business. They find that both rewards and non-rewards cardholders gain, even after accounting for higher retail prices. A bank earning money when that person buys groceries has another reason to want the account. Eliminate that revenue and the account becomes less attractive at the same borrowing terms. The adjustment could show up in the interest rate, credit limit or card approvals. Limiting interchange hurts access to credit and credit costs for the most vulnerable> Most Cards Earn Rewards—And Most Interchange Already Goes Back Out Rewards aren’t confined to a small group of people flying first class. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s latest market report says that in 2024: 80% of general purpose credit card accounts offered rewards. 92% of spending on those cards was on rewards accounts. And a separate New York Fed study finds that banks receive interchange averaging 1.82% of purchase volume and incur rewards costs averaging 1.57%. That’s about 86% of issuer interchange revenue going back out as rewards expense. Limits on credit card swipe fees actually redistribute from consumers to merchants, even as proponents seek to villify the banks. Points Aren’t The Whole Reason To Use Credit Instead Of Debit If an airline takes your money and doesn’t provide the flight, the card you used matters. So does whether a fraudulent charge has already emptied your checking account while everyone sorts out what happened. Credit cards come with federal billing dispute rights, including for purchases that weren’t delivered as agreed. With a billing error dispute, you can withhold the disputed amount during the investigation. Debit cards have fraud protections, too. But the money can already be gone from your account. Having a claim for reimbursement isn’t the same as keeping your cash available for rent while the claim gets resolved. Then there are the benefits particular cards add: purchase protection against theft or damage, extended warranties, return protection, rental-car coverage and insurance for covered travel disruptions. Interchange helps fund the card’s economics: rewards, fraud losses, dispute handling and benefits. Cutting interchange doesn’t repeal federal consumer protections athough those were imposed on an economic model that included them. And it an change what banks charge for the product, which optional benefits they offer and which customers they want. Credit cards come with federal billing dispute rights, including for purchases that weren’t delivered as agreed. With a billing error dispute, you can withhold the disputed amount during the investigation.

Debit cards have fraud protections, too. But the money can already be gone from your account. Having a claim for reimbursement isn’t the same as keeping your cash available for rent while the claim gets resolved.

Then there are the benefits particular cards add: purchase protection against theft or damage, extended warranties, return protection, rental-car coverage and insurance for covered travel disruptions.

Interchange helps fund the card’s economics: rewards, fraud losses, dispute handling and benefits. Cutting interchange doesn’t repeal federal consumer protections athough those were imposed on an economic model that included them. And it an change what banks charge for the product, which optional benefits they offer and which customers they want.

#6198. “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:

An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.

It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”

A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”

It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”

The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”

A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”

In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”

Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”

Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.

Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

#6197. Airline Lobby Chief Says Up To 99% Of Flyers Are Happy—His Own Survey Disagrees

The head of the U.S. airline lobby says 98% to 99% of passengers are “very happy.” His own organization’s survey says 72% are satisfied (28% aren’t!) and just 31% are very satisfied. It’s good to know that most people are satisfied with flying, although the sameness of business models especially in the domestic market and variable wait times at airports, long walks through terminals, and air traffic control delays are frustrating and we’re making relatively little progress. Air travel is largely safe and affordable. Chris Sununu, the former New Hampshire governor who now leads Airlines for America, made the 99% claim on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. He was arguing against a return to economic regulation and saying the industry needs to do a better job telling its success story. With Democrats retaking Congress, airline re-regulatoin becomes a target for Senators like Elizabeth Warren. Here’s What The Airline Lobby’s Research Found Airlines for America commissioned Ipsos to conduct its latest annual air-traveler survey. Overall in 2025: 31% were very satisfied. 41% were somewhat satisfied. 16% were neutral. 9% were somewhat dissatisfied. 3% were very dissatisfied. That’s 72% satisfied, up from 69% in the prior year (which is flat). 28% aren’t at least somewhat satisfied. Getting Someone There Isn’t The Same As Making Them Happy A passenger can reach their destination and still have spent hours dealing with flight changes, seat assignments, or cancellations and waiting in line to check bags. People are more happy when flights operate on-time. They’re happier when the middle seat next to them is empty. They’re happy when the employees they interact with seem not to hate their jobs. Airlines are now trying to get passengers to spend more for their product, move their loyalty and put the airline’s credit card at the top of their wallet. Delivering on-time transportation is baseline – necessary, but not sufficient. The Industry Has A Better Argument Available Sununu is right to reject a return to government deciding which airlines can fly which routes and what they can charge. Customer complaints aren’t a reason to restore that system. We need competition, fewer barriers to entry into the industry for new carriers and more innovative business models and aircraft. The airline industry has been subsidized, and it’s largely sclerotic. More regulation would make that worse – but simply denying that air travel could be better – that ‘99%’ of consumers are happy – isn’t the right case to be making.
